title: The strong law of large numbers
statement: \begin{gathered} X_1, X_2, \dots \ \text{i.i.d.}, \quad \mathbb{E}|X_1| < \infty \\ \Longrightarrow \ \bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \to \mathbb{E} X_1 \ \text{almost surely} \end{gathered}
assumptions: The X_i have the same law.
The X_i are pairwise independent (Etemadi). Full independence is the classical condition.
proof: Truncate: Y_k = X_k 1{|X_k| ≤ k}. Integrability gives Σ P(X_k ≠ Y_k) < ∞, so X_k = Y_k for all large k (Borel–Cantelli). Chebyshev's inequality on a geometric subsequence n_j = ⌊α^j⌋ with α > 1 gives almost sure convergence of the truncated means. For X ≥ 0, monotonicity covers the indices between the n_j. Then split X = X⁺ − X⁻.
reference: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Cambridge University Press, 2019, Theorem 2.4.1. N. Etemadi, An elementary proof of the strong law of large numbers, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie verw. Gebiete 55 (1981) 119–122.
counterexample: The zeta law with s = 1.8 has E[X] = ∞. Then X̄_n → ∞ almost surely, so no finite limit exists.

title: The central limit theorem and the CLT interval
statement: \begin{gathered} X_i \ \text{i.i.d.}, \quad 0 < \sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var} X_1 < \infty \\ \Longrightarrow \ \frac{\sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \Rightarrow N(0, 1) \end{gathered}
assumptions: The X_i are i.i.d.
The variance σ² is finite and positive.
The coverage 0.95 of the interval X̄_n ± 1.96 s_n/√n is a limit as n → ∞. A bound for a given n needs more, for example E|X|³ < ∞ (Berry–Esseen).
proof: Let φ be the characteristic function of X_1 − μ. Then φ(u) = 1 − σ²u²/2 + o(u²), and the characteristic function of the normalised sum is φ(t/(σ√n))^n. Its limit is e^(−t²/2). Lévy's continuity theorem gives convergence in law. Slutsky's lemma replaces σ by s_n.
reference: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., 2019, Theorem 3.4.1. B. V. Gnedenko and A. N. Kolmogorov, Limit Distributions for Sums of Independent Random Variables, Addison-Wesley, 1954.
counterexample: The zeta law with s = 2.5 has a finite mean and an infinite variance. Then (S_n − nμ)/n^(2/3) converges in law to a stable law with index 1.5, not to a normal law. Thus the CLT interval has no coverage guarantee. The block coverage in the diagnostics shows the effect in a run.

title: Consistency of the estimator and exactness of rejection
statement: \begin{gathered} \mathbb{E}|g(X)| < \infty \ \Rightarrow \ \mathbb{E}\hat\theta_n = \theta, \ \hat\theta_n \to \theta \ \text{a.s.} \\ p \le M q \ \Rightarrow \ Y \mid \text{accept} \sim p \end{gathered}
assumptions: Each replicate draws exactly from the model law.
For rejection: p and q each sum to 1, and p(k) ≤ M q(k) for every k. The acceptance uniform is independent of the proposal.
proof: Unbiasedness follows from the linearity of expectation, and consistency from the strong law. For rejection, P(accept, Y = k) = q(k) p(k)/(M q(k)) = p(k)/M. The sum over k gives P(accept) = 1/M. Divide to get P(Y = k | accept) = p(k).
reference: L. Devroye, Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation, Springer, 1986, chapter II. S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter II.
counterexample: If M is too small, the accepted values follow min(p, Mq) after normalisation, not p. The estimator is then consistent for the wrong quantity.

title: Monte Carlo error and the zero-hit bound
statement: \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_n = \frac{\sigma_g^2}{n} \\ 0 \ \text{hits in} \ n \ \Rightarrow \ p \le 1 - \alpha^{1/n} \ \text{at confidence} \ 1 - \alpha, \quad 1 - 0.05^{1/n} \approx \frac{3}{n} \end{gathered}
assumptions: The replicates are independent.
σ_g² = Var g(X) is finite for Var θ̂_n = σ_g²/n.
For the zero-hit bound, each replicate shows the event independently with the same probability p.
proof: The variance of a sum of independent terms is the sum of their variances, so Var θ̂_n = σ_g²/n for any dimension of X. For the bound: P(0 hits) = (1 − p)^n, which is at most α if and only if p ≥ 1 − α^(1/n). Thus a test at level α rejects every p above the bound.
reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation, 2007, chapter III. J. A. Hanley and A. Lippman-Hand, If nothing goes wrong, is everything all right? JAMA 249 (1983) 1743–1745.
counterexample: If replicates reuse 16 streams, the draws repeat and are not independent. The formula s/√n then understates the error by a factor near √(n/16), and the intervals cover the reference less often.

title: Variance reduction: when each method lowers the variance
statement: \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_{\mathrm{st}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k w_k \sigma_k^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_k w_k (\mu_k - \mu)^2 \\ \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}(1 + \rho), \quad \rho \le 0 \ \text{if} \ g \ \text{is monotone} \\ \min_{\beta} \operatorname{Var}(Y - \beta C) = \sigma_Y^2 \left(1 - \rho_{YC}^2\right) \\ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y^{(a)} - Y^{(b)}\right) = \sigma_a^2 + \sigma_b^2 - 2\operatorname{Cov}\left(Y^{(a)}, Y^{(b)}\right) \end{gathered}
assumptions: Stratification: the allocation n_k = w_k n is proportional to the exact stratum probabilities w_k.
Antithetic variables: X = F⁻¹(U) and X' = F⁻¹(1 − U), and g is non-decreasing or non-increasing in each uniform.
Control variates: 0 < Var C < ∞, Var Y < ∞, and μ_C is exact.
Common random numbers: the same uniforms drive both alternatives. The gain needs a positive covariance of the outputs.
proof: Stratification: the law of total variance splits σ² into the mean of the variances inside the strata and the variance of the stratum means. Proportional allocation removes the second part. Antithetic pairs: Var((Y + Y')/2) = (σ²/2)(1 + ρ) for one pair. If g is monotone, then one of g(U) and g(1 − U) increases with U and the other decreases. So their covariance is at most 0 (Chebyshev's association inequality). Control variates: Var(Y − βC) = σ_Y² − 2β Cov(Y, C) + β² Var C is smallest at β* = Cov(Y, C)/Var C, with the value σ_Y²(1 − ρ²). Common random numbers: the variance of a difference follows from the bilinearity of the covariance.
reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter V. P. Glasserman, Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering, Springer, 2004, chapter 4. A. B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, 2013, chapters 8 and 10.
counterexample: Let g be an even function of a symmetric input, such as (X − μ)² for a normal X. Then g(X') = g(X) for the antithetic partner X' = 2μ − X. Thus ρ = 1, and the pairs double the variance for the same number of evaluations.

title: Regular variation and subexponentiality
statement: \begin{gathered} \bar F(x) = x^{-\alpha}\ell(x), \ \ \frac{\ell(tx)}{\ell(x)} \to 1 \ (x \to \infty) \ \text{for every} \ t > 0 \ \ \Longrightarrow \\ \mathbb{P}(X_1 + \dots + X_n > x) \sim n\,\bar F(x) \sim \mathbb{P}\left(\max_{i \le n} X_i > x\right) \ \ (x \to \infty) \end{gathered}
assumptions: X_1, …, X_n are nonnegative and i.i.d. with the law F, for a fixed n.
The tail is regularly varying with an index α > 0: F̄(x) = x^(−α) ℓ(x) with ℓ slowly varying. Then F is subexponential.
A subexponential law has P(X_1 + X_2 > x) ~ 2 F̄(x), by definition. It includes the lognormal law and the Weibull law with k < 1, which are not regularly varying.
proof: The lower bound: {max X_i > x} ⊂ {S_n > x} when the X_i are positive, and P(max X_i > x) = 1 − F(x)^n ~ n F̄(x). The upper bound for n = 2: if X_1 + X_2 > x, then X_1 > (1 − ε)x, or X_2 > (1 − ε)x, or both are above εx. The first two events have probability at most 2 F̄((1 − ε)x) ~ 2(1 − ε)^(−α) F̄(x). The third has probability F̄(εx)², which is o(F̄(x)). Let ε → 0. Induction on n gives the general case.
reference: P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, section 1.3 and appendix A3. N. H. Bingham, C. M. Goldie and J. L. Teugels, Regular Variation, Cambridge University Press, 1987.
counterexample: For the standard exponential law, P(X_1 + X_2 > x) = (1 + x) e^(−x), so the ratio to 2 P(X > x) is (1 + x)/2 → ∞. A large sum of light-tailed values comes from many moderate values, not from one large value.

title: Extreme-value limits and domains of attraction
statement: \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}\left(\frac{M_n - b_n}{a_n} \le x\right) = F(a_n x + b_n)^n \to G(x) \ \text{non-degenerate} \ \Longrightarrow \\ G(x) = \exp\left(-(1 + \xi x)^{-1/\xi}\right), \ 1 + \xi x > 0, \ \text{for some} \ \xi \in \mathbb{R} \end{gathered}
assumptions: M_n is the maximum of n i.i.d. values with the law F, and a_n > 0 and b_n are constants.
G is non-degenerate: it is not a point mass. Then G is a GEV law, up to a change of location and scale (Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko).

Domains of attraction: ξ > 0 if and only if F̄ is regularly varying with index 1/ξ. ξ < 0 if and only if the end point x_F is finite and F̄(x_F − 1/x) is regularly varying with index −1/ξ. ξ = 0 holds for laws such as the normal, exponential, Gompertz and lognormal laws.
proof: Max-stability: let F^n(a_n x + b_n) → G. Then for each k, the maximum of k blocks of n values gives G^k(α_k x + β_k) = G(x). By the convergence of types (Khinchine), G is max-stable. Take logarithms: −log G is a positive decreasing function that satisfies a Cauchy-type functional equation. Its only solutions are (1 + ξx)^(−1/ξ) and e^(−x) (the case ξ = 0).
reference: P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, theorems 3.2.3 and 3.3.7. L. de Haan and A. Ferreira, Extreme Value Theory: An Introduction, Springer, 2006, theorem 1.1.3. S. Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values, Springer, 2001, chapter 3.
counterexample: The Poisson law is in no domain of attraction. P(X = k)/P(X ≥ k) does not tend to 0, so no constants a_n and b_n give a non-degenerate limit of its maxima. The geometric law has the same problem. A discrete law needs this jump condition before the theorem can apply.

title: Threshold exceedances, maxima and sums
statement: \begin{gathered} F \in \mathrm{MDA}(G_\xi) \iff \lim_{u \to x_F} \ \sup_{0 < y < x_F - u} \left| \mathbb{P}(X - u \le y \mid X > u) - H_{\xi, \sigma(u)}(y) \right| = 0 \\ H_{\xi,\sigma}(y) = 1 - (1 + \xi y/\sigma)^{-1/\xi}, \qquad \text{for } X \sim H_{\xi,\sigma}: \ \mathbb{E}[X - u \mid X > u] = \frac{\sigma + \xi u}{1 - \xi} \ (\xi < 1) \end{gathered}
assumptions: X has the law F with the upper end point x_F, which can be ∞.
F is in the maximum domain of attraction of the GEV law G_ξ, for a suitable function σ(u) > 0 (Pickands–Balkema–de Haan).
The GPD H_ξ,σ is threshold stable: its excess over u is GPD with the same ξ and the scale σ + ξu. Thus its mean excess is linear in u for ξ < 1.
proof: Take logarithms of F^n(a_n x + b_n) → G_ξ(x): n F̄(a_n x + b_n) → (1 + ξx)^(−1/ξ). Divide the value at x + y by the value at x. Put u = a_n x + b_n. Then F̄(u + a_n y)/F̄(u) → (1 + ξy/(1 + ξx))^(−1/ξ). This is the GPD survival function with the scale σ(u) = a_n(1 + ξx). Monotonicity of F̄ makes the convergence uniform in y.
reference: A. A. Balkema and L. de Haan, Residual life time at great age, Annals of Probability 2 (1974) 792–804. J. Pickands, Statistical inference using extreme order statistics, Annals of Statistics 3 (1975) 119–131. P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, theorem 3.4.13.
counterexample: The theorem is a limit. At a fixed threshold the excess law of the lognormal law is not a GPD law. The lognormal law is in the domain ξ = 0, but its mean excess still increases with u. Thus a fit at a practical threshold often shows an apparent ξ > 0. The Poisson law, which is in no domain of attraction, has no GPD limit at all.

title: Ergodicity, mixing, and time and ensemble averages
statement: \begin{gathered} (X_n) \text{ irreducible, positive recurrent with stationary law } \pi: \quad \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(X_k) \to \sum_x \pi(x) f(x) \ \text{a.s. for every } X_0 \\ \text{and, if also aperiodic:} \quad \lVert P^n(x, \cdot) - \pi \rVert_{TV} \to 0 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The chain is irreducible: each state reaches each other state.
It is positive recurrent. A finite irreducible chain always is. Then the stationary law π is unique.
f has a finite mean under π. The convergence of the law Pⁿ(x, ·) needs aperiodicity. The convergence of the time average does not.
For a general stationary process, Birkhoff's theorem gives the limit E[f | invariant σ-field] of the time average. This limit equals the ensemble average when the process is ergodic.
proof: Split the path at the returns to a state x. The excursions between returns are i.i.d. (strong Markov property), and positive recurrence gives them a finite mean length E_x τ_x = 1/π(x). The strong law of large numbers applies to the sums of f over the excursions and to their lengths. The ratio of the two sums gives Σ π f. For the law, couple two copies of the chain, one started from π, until they meet at a time T. Aperiodicity and irreducibility make T finite, and ‖Pⁿ(x, ·) − π‖_TV ≤ P(T > n).
reference: J. R. Norris, Markov Chains, Cambridge University Press, 1997, theorems 1.8.3 and 1.10.2. D. A. Levin and Y. Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2017, chapter 4. G. D. Birkhoff, Proof of the ergodic theorem, PNAS 17 (1931) 656–660.
counterexample: Geometric Brownian motion is not stationary. Let μ < σ²/2. Then (log S_t)/t → μ − σ²/2 < 0 almost surely, so almost every path tends to 0. But when μ > 0, the ensemble average E S_t = S_0 e^(μt) grows. The mean of many paths and the long-run growth of one path differ. A reducible chain with two closed classes also has a time average that depends on X_0.

title: Sklar's theorem and copulas
statement: \begin{gathered} F(x_1, \dots, x_d) = C\left(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d)\right) \text{ for a copula } C, \text{ unique on } \operatorname{Ran} F_1 \times \dots \times \operatorname{Ran} F_d \\ U \sim C, \ X_j = F_j^{-1}(U_j) \ \Longrightarrow \ X \sim F, \qquad \tau, \ \lambda_U, \ \lambda_L \text{ depend on } C \text{ only} \end{gathered}
assumptions: F is a d-dimensional CDF with the margins F_1, …, F_d.
A copula is a CDF on [0, 1]^d with uniform margins.
C is unique when every margin is continuous. A discrete margin leaves C free outside the range of the margins, so discrete data do not identify their copula.
λ_U = lim_{q→1} P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q) and λ_L = lim_{q→0} P(U_2 ≤ q | U_1 ≤ q), where the limits exist.
proof: For continuous margins, U_j = F_j(X_j) is uniform, and C is the CDF of U. Then F(x) = P(U_j ≤ F_j(x_j) for all j) = C(F_1(x_1), …). Conversely, F_j^(−1)(U_j) ≤ x_j if and only if U_j ≤ F_j(x_j), so the quantile transform of U ~ C has the CDF C(F_1, …, F_d). Kendall's tau and the tail coefficients are invariant under strictly increasing maps of the components, so they depend only on C. For discrete margins, extend F by interpolation to a continuous CDF on the range.
reference: A. Sklar, Fonctions de répartition à n dimensions et leurs marges, Publ. Inst. Statist. Univ. Paris 8 (1959) 229–231. R. B. Nelsen, An Introduction to Copulas, 2nd ed., Springer, 2006, theorems 2.10.9 and 5.1.9. A. J. McNeil, R. Frey and P. Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management, revised ed., Princeton University Press, 2015, chapter 7.
counterexample: The Gaussian and the Student t copula with the same correlation ρ = 0.5 have the same Kendall's tau, (2/π) arcsin ρ = 1/3. But λ_U = 0 for the Gaussian copula, and λ_U is about 0.25 for the t copula with ν = 4. The same margins and the same tau thus give different probabilities of joint extremes.

title: Multilevel Monte Carlo and discretisation bias
statement: \begin{gathered} |\mathbb{E}[P_l - P]| \le c_1 2^{-\alpha l}, \ V_l \le c_2 2^{-\beta l}, \ C_l \le c_3 2^{\gamma l}, \ \alpha \ge \tfrac12 \min(\beta, \gamma) \\ \Longrightarrow \ \exists L, N_l: \ \mathbb{E}\left[(\hat\theta - \mathbb{E}P)^2\right] < \varepsilon^2 \ \text{with cost} \ \le c_4 \begin{cases} \varepsilon^{-2} & \beta > \gamma \\ \varepsilon^{-2} (\log \varepsilon)^2 & \beta = \gamma \\ \varepsilon^{-2 - (\gamma - \beta)/\alpha} & \beta < \gamma \end{cases} \end{gathered}
assumptions: P_l is the quantity on the grid of level l, and P is its limit. The correction Y_l = P_l − P_(l−1) uses P_l and P_(l−1) on the same Brownian path.
The rates α, β and γ hold for every level. For the Euler–Maruyama scheme and a Lipschitz payoff, α = β = γ = 1.
The levels are independent, so the variance of the estimator is Σ V_l/N_l.
The mean square error is the sum of the Monte Carlo variance and the squared bias: E[(θ̂ − EP)²] = Σ V_l/N_l + (E P_L − E P)².
proof: Choose L with c_1 2^(−αL) ≤ ε/√2, so the squared bias is at most ε²/2. Minimise the cost Σ N_l C_l under the constraint Σ V_l/N_l ≤ ε²/2 with a Lagrange multiplier: N_l ∝ √(V_l/C_l). The cost is then 2ε^(−2)(Σ √(V_l C_l))². The sum Σ 2^((γ−β)l/2) stays bounded when β > γ, grows as L when β = γ, and grows as 2^((γ−β)L/2) when β < γ. With L ≈ log2(1/ε)/α this gives the three cases.
reference: M. B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo path simulation, Operations Research 56 (2008) 607–617. M. B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, theorem 1. P. E. Kloeden and E. Platen, Numerical Solution of Stochastic Differential Equations, Springer, 1992, chapters 10 and 14.
counterexample: Take the indicator that Brownian motion reaches a level, checked only at the grid times. A fine and a coarse path disagree with a probability of order 2^(−l/2), so β = 1/2 < γ = 1. The cost then grows as ε^(−3) up to a log factor, near the cost of plain Monte Carlo. The interval of a plain run on one grid also says nothing about its bias: a smaller interval does not reduce the monitoring bias.

title: Large deviations and the rate function
statement: \begin{gathered} \Lambda(\theta) = \log \mathbb E\, e^{\theta X_1}, \quad I(a) = \sup_{\theta} \left(\theta a - \Lambda(\theta)\right) \\ \Longrightarrow \ \frac{1}{n}\log \mathbb P(S_n \ge na) \to -I(a) \ \text{and} \ \mathbb P(S_n \ge na) \le e^{-n I(a)} \ \text{for } a > \mathbb E X_1 \end{gathered}
assumptions: X_1, X_2, … are i.i.d. real random variables, and S_n = X_1 + … + X_n.
Λ(θ) < ∞ for θ in a neighbourhood of 0, and a is inside the range of Λ'. The upper bound (Chernoff) holds for every n.
For exponential jumps with mean μ, I(a) = a/μ − 1 − log(a/μ) and θ* = 1/μ − 1/a. Bahadur and Rao refine the limit: P(S_n ≥ na) ~ e^(−nI(a)) / (θ* σ_a √(2πn)).
proof: Upper bound: for θ ≥ 0, Markov's inequality gives P(S_n ≥ na) ≤ E e^(θS_n) e^(−θna) = e^(−n(θa − Λ(θ))). Take the best θ. Lower bound: change the measure to the tilted law dF_θ* = e^(θ*x − Λ(θ*)) dF, under which the mean is a. Then P(S_n ≥ na) = E_θ*[e^(−θ*S_n + nΛ(θ*)); S_n ≥ na]. Under the tilted law, S_n stays within √n of na with a probability bounded below (CLT). This gives the rate −I(a).
reference: A. Dembo and O. Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, theorem 2.2.3. R. R. Bahadur and R. Ranga Rao, Ann. Math. Statist. 31 (1960) 1015–1027.
counterexample: For Pareto II jumps, Λ(θ) = ∞ for every θ > 0, so I(a) = 0 above the mean. P(S_n > na) then decays as a power of n, about n P(X > n(a − μ)), not exponentially. The Chernoff bound gives only the value 1.

title: Change of measure and exponential tilting
statement: \begin{gathered} \mathbb E_f\!\left[h(X)\right] = \mathbb E_g\!\left[h(X)\,\frac{f(X)}{g(X)}\right] \ \text{when } g > 0 \text{ wherever } h f \ne 0; \\ \operatorname{Var}_g = \mathbb E_g\!\left[h^2 \tfrac{f^2}{g^2}\right] - \left(\mathbb E_f h\right)^2, \quad g^* = \frac{|h| f}{\mathbb E_f |h|} \ \text{has zero variance for } h \ge 0 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The proposal g is positive wherever h f is not zero: then the weighted estimator has no bias.
The variance is finite only if E_g[h² f²/g²] < ∞. A proposal with a lighter tail than f can make it infinite.

An exponential tilt dF_θ = e^(θx − Λ(θ)) dF exists only when Λ(θ) < ∞. For the tail of a sum it is logarithmically efficient: the second moment decays at twice the rate of p (Sadowsky and Bucklew, 1990).
proof: The identity is ∫ h f = ∫ h (f/g) g on the set where g > 0. This set contains every point where h f ≠ 0. The zero-variance law follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: E_g[h² f²/g²] ≥ (E_f |h|)², with equality when g ∝ |h| f. For the tail of a sum, the tilt θ* makes the weight e^(nΛ(θ*) − θ*S_n) at most e^(−nI(a)) on the event. Thus the second moment is at most e^(−2nI(a)).
reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter VI. J. S. Sadowsky and J. A. Bucklew, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 36 (1990) 579–588. D. Siegmund, Ann. Statist. 4 (1976) 673–684.
counterexample: For Pareto II claims, an exponential proposal with any mean gives f/g → ∞ as x → ∞, and E_g[f²/g²; S > b] = ∞. The estimator has no bias, but its variance is infinite. Most replications give a value below p, and a few replications give very large values.

title: Ruin theory: the Cramér–Lundberg model
statement: \begin{gathered} U(t) = u + ct - \sum_{i=1}^{N(t)} X_i, \quad \psi(u) = \mathbb P\!\left(\inf_{t \ge 0} U(t) < 0\right), \quad \lambda\left(\mathbb E e^{RX} - 1\right) = cR \\ \Longrightarrow \ \psi(u) \le e^{-Ru} \ \text{(Lundberg)}, \qquad \psi(u) \sim C e^{-Ru} \ \text{(Cramér)}, \qquad \psi(u) = \rho\, e^{-(1-\rho)u/\mu} \ \text{for exponential } X \text{ with mean } \mu \end{gathered}
assumptions: The claims arrive as a Poisson process with rate λ, and their sizes X_i are i.i.d., positive and independent of the arrivals.
The net profit condition ρ = λ E X / c < 1 holds. Else ψ(u) = 1 for every u.
The equation λ(E e^(RX) − 1) = cR has a positive root R, the adjustment coefficient. This needs E e^(θX) < ∞ for some θ > 0, but that alone is not enough. No root exists for heavy-tailed claims.
proof: The process e^(−R U(t)) is a martingale when λ(E e^(RX) − 1) = cR. At the time of ruin τ, U(τ) < 0. The optional stopping theorem then gives e^(−Ru) = E[e^(−RU(τ)); τ < ∞] ≥ P(τ < ∞), which is the Lundberg inequality. Under the measure tilted by R, ruin is certain, and ψ(u) = e^(−Ru) E_R[e^(−Rξ)] with the overshoot ξ. The renewal theorem gives the constant C. For exponential claims, the overshoot is exponential, and this gives the exact formula.
reference: S. Asmussen and H. Albrecher, Ruin Probabilities, 2nd ed., World Scientific, 2010, chapters I and IV. D. Siegmund, Ann. Statist. 4 (1976) 673–684.
counterexample: With Pareto II claims (α = 2.5), E e^(θX) = ∞ for every θ > 0, so no R exists and no exponential bound holds: ψ(u) decays as u^(−1.5). Double the capital, and the ruin probability falls by a factor of about 2.8, not by a factor that grows exponentially in u.

title: The Pollaczek–Khinchine formula and subexponential ruin
statement: \begin{gathered} \psi(u) = (1-\rho)\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \rho^k\, \overline{F_I^{*k}}(u), \qquad F_I(x) = \frac{1}{\mu}\int_0^x \bar F(y)\,dy \\ F_I \ \text{subexponential} \ \Longrightarrow \ \psi(u) \sim \frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\bar F_I(u) \quad (u \to \infty) \end{gathered}
assumptions: The Cramér–Lundberg model with ρ = λμ/c < 1 and a finite mean claim μ.

The integrated-tail law F_I is the law of a ladder height. A ladder height is the amount by which the maximum of the claim surplus grows at a new record. For Pareto II claims with index α, F_I is Pareto II with index α − 1.
The asymptotic needs F_I subexponential (Embrechts and Veraverbeke, 1982). It is a limit as u → ∞, not a bound at a given u.
proof: The maximum M of the claim surplus is the sum of its ladder heights. A new record occurs with probability ρ. Each record adds an independent ladder height with law F_I (Wiener–Hopf factorisation). Thus M is a geometric sum, and ψ(u) = P(M > u). For a subexponential F_I, P(Y_1 + … + Y_k > u) ~ k F̄_I(u). Dominated convergence (Kesten's bound) then gives Σ (1 − ρ) ρ^k k F̄_I(u) = ρ/(1 − ρ) F̄_I(u).
reference: P. Embrechts and N. Veraverbeke, Insurance Math. Econom. 1 (1982) 55–72. P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events, Springer, 1997, section 1.4. S. Asmussen and D. P. Kroese, Adv. Appl. Probab. 38 (2006) 545–558.
counterexample: For exponential claims, F_I is exponential, which is not subexponential. Then ψ(u) = ρ e^(−(1−ρ)u/μ), while ρ/(1 − ρ) F̄_I(u) = ρ/(1 − ρ) e^(−u/μ): the two differ by a factor that grows exponentially in u.

title: Dependence in extremes
statement: \begin{gathered} \lambda_U = \lim_{q \to 1} \mathbb P\!\left(U_2 > q \mid U_1 > q\right) \\ \text{Gaussian copula, } |r| < 1: \ \lambda_U = 0; \qquad \text{Gumbel copula, } \theta \ge 1: \ \lambda_U = 2 - 2^{1/\theta}, \quad \tau = 1 - 1/\theta \end{gathered}
assumptions: (U_1, U_2) has uniform margins and the copula C, so P(U_1 > q, U_2 > q) = 1 − 2q + C(q, q).
The limit exists. λ_U depends on the copula only, not on the margins.

Kendall's τ and the linear correlation summarise the dependence over the whole law. τ depends only on the copula, but the correlation also depends on the margins. λ_U measures only the joint extremes.
proof: For the Gumbel copula, C(q, q) = exp(−(2(−log q)^θ)^(1/θ)) = q^(2^(1/θ)). Then (1 − 2q + q^(2^(1/θ)))/(1 − q) → 2 − 2^(1/θ) as q → 1, by l'Hôpital's rule. For the Gaussian copula, P(Z_2 > z | Z_1 > z) → 0 as z → ∞ when |r| < 1 (Sibuya, 1960). The reason is that Z_2 given Z_1 = z is normal with mean rz, and rz grows more slowly than z.
reference: A. J. McNeil, R. Frey and P. Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management, revised ed., Princeton University Press, 2015, section 7.2.4. M. Sibuya, Ann. Inst. Statist. Math. 11 (1960) 195–210.
counterexample: The Gaussian and the Gumbel copulas with τ = 0.5 have the same Kendall's τ. But λ_U = 0 for the Gaussian copula and 2 − √2 = 0.59 for the Gumbel copula. In the catastrophe test, the common event loss also makes the insurers lose together. Thus the copula of the shares changes the probability of a systemic ruin less than λ_U suggests. A tail coefficient of one part of a model is not a property of the whole model.

title: Tail sensitivity and ruin, in an explicit model
statement: \begin{gathered} X \sim \text{Pareto II}(\sigma, \alpha): \quad \operatorname{VaR}_q = \sigma\left((1-q)^{-1/\alpha} - 1\right), \quad \operatorname{ES}_q = \frac{\alpha \operatorname{VaR}_q + \sigma}{\alpha - 1} \ (\alpha > 1), \quad \operatorname{ES}_q = \infty \ (\alpha \le 1) \\ \frac{\partial \log \operatorname{ES}_q}{\partial \alpha} \to -\infty \ \text{as } \alpha \downarrow 1; \qquad \mathbb P(\text{ruin within } k \text{ periods}) = 1 - (1-p)^k \to 1 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The loss has a Pareto II law with a known tail index α, and the periods are independent with the same ruin probability p > 0.
The value at risk and the expected shortfall are at the level q. ES_q = E[X | X > VaR_q] is finite only when E X is finite.
Taleb's arguments about fat tails and ruin are interpretations. The page states only the facts of this model, and it does not present an interpretation as a theorem.
proof: For the Pareto II law, P(X > x) = (1 + x/σ)^(−α), which inverts to VaR_q. Given X > v, X − v is Pareto II with scale σ + v and the same α, so E[X − v | X > v] = (σ + v)/(α − 1), which gives ES_q. Thus log ES_q = log(α VaR_q + σ) − log(α − 1). The first term has a bounded derivative near α = 1, and the derivative of −log(α − 1) is −1/(α − 1), which tends to −∞ as α ↓ 1. The probability of no ruin in k independent periods is (1 − p)^k, which tends to 0 for any p > 0.
reference: P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events, Springer, 1997, chapter 6. N. N. Taleb, Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails, STEM Academic Press, 2020 (the interpretation). A. J. McNeil, R. Frey and P. Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management, 2015, section 2.3.
counterexample: A sample mean of Pareto II losses with α = 0.9 is always finite, but E X = ∞. Thus a finite sample gives a finite ES estimate for a law whose ES is infinite. In the opposite direction, a truncation at a largest possible loss makes every moment finite, but no finite sample can show where the truncation is.

title: Ergodic averages and the Markov chain CLT
statement: \begin{gathered} P \text{ Harris ergodic with } \pi P = \pi, \ \pi|g| < \infty \ \Longrightarrow \ \bar g_n = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} g(X_i) \to \pi(g) \ \text{a.s., from any start} \\ \text{geometric ergodicity}, \ \pi|g|^{2+\delta} < \infty \ \Longrightarrow \ \sqrt n\,(\bar g_n - \pi g) \Rightarrow N(0, \sigma_g^2), \quad \sigma_g^2 = \operatorname{Var}_\pi g \Bigl(1 + 2\sum_{k \ge 1} \rho_k\Bigr) = \operatorname{Var}_\pi g \cdot \tau, \quad \mathrm{ESS} = n / \tau \end{gathered}
assumptions: The kernel P keeps π stationary. Metropolis–Hastings and each coordinate update of the Gibbs sweep satisfy detailed balance, so the sweep keeps π stationary. In Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, the leapfrog map with a momentum flip keeps volume and is its own inverse. With the Metropolis step, the chain keeps π stationary.
The chain is φ-irreducible, aperiodic and Harris recurrent, so it is Harris ergodic.
For the central limit theorem: geometric ergodicity and π|g|^(2+δ) < ∞ for some δ > 0, or a reversible chain with π g² < ∞ and a finite asymptotic variance.
proof: For the ergodic theorem, Nummelin's splitting gives regeneration times. The sums of g between regenerations are i.i.d., and the strong law of large numbers applies to them. For the central limit theorem, solve the Poisson equation ĝ − Pĝ = g − π g. Then the sum of g(X_i) − π g is a martingale plus the remainder ĝ(X₀) − ĝ(X_n), which is small compared with √n. The martingale central limit theorem applies. The variance of the martingale increments is Var_π g (1 + 2 Σ ρ_k).
reference: G. O. Roberts and J. S. Rosenthal, General state space Markov chains and MCMC algorithms, Probability Surveys 1 (2004) 20–71. G. L. Jones, On the Markov chain central limit theorem, Probability Surveys 1 (2004) 299–320. C. J. Geyer, Practical Markov chain Monte Carlo, Statistical Science 7 (1992) 473–483. A. Vehtari, A. Gelman, D. Simpson, B. Carpenter and P.-C. Bürkner, Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: an improved R-hat, Bayesian Analysis 16 (2021) 667–718.
counterexample: A random walk on two modes 11 units apart is ergodic, so the theorem holds. But the expected time to cross between the modes is far longer than any run. Chains that start in one mode agree with each other: split R-hat is near 1 and the ESS is large. But the estimate of P(x₁ + x₂ > 0) is near 0, and the exact value is 0.7. A theorem about n → ∞ says nothing about the n of one run, and the ESS is a diagnostic, not a proof of convergence.

title: Importance weights, resampling and the unbiased likelihood
statement: \begin{gathered} \hat Z_T = \prod_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{i=1}^{N} W_{t-1}^i\, g_t(x_t^i), \qquad \mathbb E\,\hat Z_T = p(y_{1:T}) \ \text{for every } N \ge 1 \\ \mathrm{ESS}_t = \Bigl(\sum_i W_t^i\Bigr)^2 \Big/ \sum_i (W_t^i)^2 \in [1, N] \end{gathered}
assumptions: The particles move with the transition law f of the model, and g_t(x) = p(y_t | x_t = x) is the observation density.
The resampling scheme has no bias: given the weights, the expected number of copies of particle i is N W_i. Multinomial, stratified, systematic and residual resampling have this property.

E Ẑ_T = p(y_{1:T}) needs only these conditions. Error bounds for the filter law that do not grow with T need more: bounded potentials g_t and a mixing transition. Then the relative variance of Ẑ_T grows linearly in T.
proof: Let F_t be the history of the particle system up to time t. The resampling has no bias. Thus, given F_(t−1), each new particle comes from the mixture Σ_i W_(t−1)^i f(· | x_(t−1)^i). Thus E[Σ_i W_(t−1)^i g_t(x_t^i) | F_(t−1)] = Σ_i W_(t−1)^i ∫ f(x | x_(t−1)^i) g_t(x) dx. By induction on t, E[Ẑ_t Σ_i W_t^i φ(x_t^i)] = ∫ φ(x) p(x_t = x, y_(1:t)) dx for every bounded φ. Take φ = 1 at t = T. The result is p(y_(1:T)).
reference: P. Del Moral, Feynman–Kac Formulae: Genealogical and Interacting Particle Systems with Applications, Springer, 2004. C. Andrieu, A. Doucet and R. Holenstein, Particle Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 72 (2010) 269–342. A. Kong, J. S. Liu and W. H. Wong, Sequential imputations and Bayesian missing data problems, Journal of the American Statistical Association 89 (1994) 278–288. N. Chopin and O. Papaspiliopoulos, An Introduction to Sequential Monte Carlo, Springer, 2020.
counterexample: Without resampling the estimator is still unbiased, but the variance of the weights grows about exponentially in T. After a few steps, one particle has almost all the weight, and the ESS is near 1. In most runs Ẑ is far below p(y_(1:T)). The mean is right only because rare runs give very large values. Also log Ẑ has a negative bias for every scheme, because log is concave.

title: Randomised quasi-Monte Carlo: no bias and a smaller variance
statement: \begin{gathered} \Bigl|\frac1n \sum_{i} f(u_i) - \int_{[0,1)^d} f\Bigr| \le V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)\, D_n^*(u_1, \dots, u_n) \quad \text{(Koksma–Hlawka)} \\ \text{scrambled } (t, m, d)\text{-net in base 2}, \ n = 2^m: \ \mathbb E \hat I = I, \quad \operatorname{Var} \hat I \le 2^t 3^d \, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}, \quad \operatorname{Var} \hat I = o(1/n) \ \text{for } f \in L^2 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The points are the first 2^m points of a Sobol sequence, a (t, m, d)-net in base 2, with Owen's nested uniform scramble. Owen (2003) shows that Matoušek's random linear scramble with a digital shift, which this page uses, has the same variance.
f is square-integrable on the unit cube. σ² is its variance: the variance of independent sampling with one point.
For smooth f, with the condition that Owen (1997) states, Var Î = O(n^(−3) (log n)^(d−1)). A jump that is not parallel to the axes removes this rate.
proof: Expand f in base-2 Haar wavelets, grouped by the resolution k = (k_1, …, k_d) in each coordinate. The scramble makes each point uniform, so Î has no bias, and it makes the contributions of different groups uncorrelated. Thus Var Î = Σ_k Γ_k σ_k² / n, where σ_k² is the variance of f in group k. The net property gives Γ_k = 0 for groups with |k| ≤ m − t, and Γ_k ≤ 2^t 3^d for all k. The groups with Γ_k ≠ 0 carry a variance that tends to 0, so n Var Î → 0.
reference: A. B. Owen, Monte Carlo variance of scrambled net quadrature, SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 34 (1997) 1884–1910. A. B. Owen, Scrambled net variance for integrals of smooth functions, Annals of Statistics 25 (1997) 1541–1562. J. Matoušek, On the L2-discrepancy for anchored boxes, Journal of Complexity 14 (1998) 527–556. A. B. Owen, Variance with alternative scramblings of digital nets, ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation 13 (2003) 363–378. S. Joe and F. Y. Kuo, Constructing Sobol sequences with better two-dimensional projections, SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 30 (2008) 2635–2654.
counterexample: The indicator that a sum of 8 uniforms is above 5 jumps along a slanted plane, so V_HK = ∞ and the Koksma–Hlawka bound is empty. The scrambled points still have no bias and a smaller variance. But the variance ratio against independent points is about 5, against more than 10,000 for the smooth peak. Without randomisation the points give one deterministic value, and repeated runs cannot estimate its error.

title: Metastability: exit times and the Arrhenius law
statement: \begin{gathered} \lim_{T \to 0} T \log \mathbb E_m[\tau] = V_m, \qquad \tau = \min\{t : V(X_t) < V(m)\} \\ \frac{\tau}{\mathbb E_m[\tau]} \Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(1) \quad (T \to 0) \end{gathered}
assumptions: The state space is finite and the Metropolis chain at temperature T has a symmetric, irreducible proposal.
m is a local minimum, and V_m is its stability level. V_m is the least barrier on a path from m to a state with a lower energy.
For the exponential law, m is the only state with the largest stability level, other than the global minima.
proof: A path of the chain has a probability of order exp(−C/T) (Freidlin and Wentzell). Here C is the sum of the rises of energy along the path. The cheapest way out of the well of m climbs V_m, so one attempt to leave succeeds with a probability of order exp(−V_m/T). The chain comes back to m many times between attempts, so the number of attempts is nearly geometric. A geometric number of nearly independent attempts gives the exponential law, and its mean gives the rate.
reference: E. Olivieri and M. E. Vares, Large Deviations and Metastability, Cambridge University Press, 2005, chapter 6. F. Manzo, F. R. Nardi, E. Olivieri and E. Scoppola, On the essential features of metastability: tunnelling time and critical configurations, Journal of Statistical Physics 115 (2004) 591–642. M. Cassandro, A. Galves, E. Olivieri and M. E. Vares, Metastable behavior of stochastic dynamics: a pathwise approach, Journal of Statistical Physics 35 (1984) 603–634.
counterexample: The theorem gives a limit as T → 0, not a value at a fixed T. On the tilted double well, V_m = 0.758. But between T = 0.12 and T = 0.3, the exact means give a slope of about 0.57. The prefactor of exp(V_m/T) changes with T. A narrow passage over the barrier changes the prefactor by orders of magnitude and leaves the limit the same.

title: Simulated annealing: Hajek's cooling theorem
statement: T_k \downarrow 0: \quad \mathbb P(X_k \in S^\ast) \to 1 \iff \sum_{k} e^{-d^\ast / T_k} = \infty; \qquad T_k = \frac{c}{\log(k+2)}: \ \iff c \ge d^\ast
assumptions: The state space is finite and connected, and the proposal is weakly reversible, for example symmetric.
The temperatures T_k decrease to 0.
S* is the set of global minima. d* is the largest depth of a local minimum that is not global, which is the barrier it must climb to reach a lower state.
proof: To leave the deepest well that is not global, the chain must climb d*. At step k it does so with a probability of order exp(−d*/T_k). If the sum of these probabilities is finite, then with a positive probability the chain never leaves, as in the Borel–Cantelli lemma. If the sum is infinite, the chain leaves every such well again and again. Then the low temperatures make the time in the global minima dominate.
reference: B. Hajek, Cooling schedules for optimal annealing, Mathematics of Operations Research 13 (1988) 311–329. S. Kirkpatrick, C. D. Gelatt and M. P. Vecchi, Optimization by simulated annealing, Science 220 (1983) 671–680.
counterexample: A geometric schedule T_k = T_0 α^k has a finite sum Σ exp(−d*/T_k). Thus the chain can stay for ever in a well that is not global. The theorem also says nothing at a finite K. On three wells, the logarithmic schedule with c = d* meets the condition. But in 65,536 steps it leaves the start well in only a few replicates.

title: Scale transformations: Dhar's exact results and the finite-size scaling hypothesis
statement: \begin{gathered} \pi = \text{uniform on the } \det\Delta \text{ recurrent configurations}, \qquad \mathbb E[n_j \mid \text{grain at } i] = (\Delta^{-1})_{ij} \\ \langle s \rangle = \tfrac{1}{N}\,\mathbf 1^{\top}\Delta^{-1}\mathbf 1 \propto L^2; \qquad P_L(s) = s^{-\tau} F(s/L^{D}) \ \text{is a hypothesis} \end{gathered}
assumptions: The BTW rule with an open boundary, no bulk dissipation and one grain at a uniform random site for each drive.
The chain is in its stationary state: the configurations are recurrent.
Δ is the toppling matrix: 4 on the diagonal and −1 for each pair of neighbours.
proof: The addition operators commute (the abelian property), and on the recurrent configurations they are invertible. They form a group with det Δ elements that acts on the recurrent set with one orbit, so the stationary law is uniform. After a grain at i, the new configuration is z + e_i − Δ n, where n counts the topplings at each site. In the stationary state the mean of z does not change, so Δ E[n] = e_i. The row sums of Δ^(−1) are mean exit times of a random walk from the box divided by 4, which grow like L².
reference: D. Dhar, Self-organized critical state of sandpile automaton models, Physical Review Letters 64 (1990) 1613–1616. D. Dhar, Theoretical studies of self-organized criticality, Physica A 369 (2006) 29–70. C. Tebaldi, M. De Menech and A. L. Stella, Multifractal scaling in the Bak–Tang–Wiesenfeld sandpile and edge events, Physical Review Letters 83 (1999) 3952–3955.
counterexample: The exact results fix the mean, not the law of the sizes. Simple finite-size scaling with one pair τ and D is a hypothesis. For the BTW rule in two dimensions, the exponents σ(q) of the moments are not linear in q (Tebaldi, De Menech and Stella 1999). A collapse that looks good on lattices up to 64 does not establish the hypothesis or a universality class.

title: Sornette's view: self-organised criticality as a tuned critical point
statement: \Delta_\varepsilon = 4I - (1-\varepsilon)A \ \text{on the torus}: \quad \Delta_\varepsilon \mathbf 1 = 4\varepsilon\,\mathbf 1 \ \Longrightarrow \ \langle s \rangle = \frac{1}{4\varepsilon} \ \text{for every } L
assumptions: The BTW rule on a periodic lattice, with one grain at a random site for each drive.
A toppling loses each grain that it moves with probability ε > 0, independently of the other grains.
The view of Sornette, Johansen and Dornic is an interpretation of models of this kind, not a theorem about natural systems.
proof: In the stationary state the mean number of topplings n satisfies Δ_ε E[n] = (1/N) 1 for a uniform random drive, as in Dhar's argument. On the torus every row of Δ_ε sums to 4 − 4(1 − ε) = 4ε, so Δ_ε^(−1) 1 = 1/(4ε) at every site. Thus the mean size stays finite at every L, and it grows without bound only as ε → 0. The dissipation is a control parameter, and the critical point is at ε = 0.
reference: D. Sornette, A. Johansen and I. Dornic, Mapping self-organized criticality onto criticality, Journal de Physique I 5 (1995) 325–335. D. Sornette, Critical Phenomena in Natural Sciences, 2nd ed., Springer, 2006, chapter 15. R. Dickman, A. Vespignani and S. Zapperi, Self-organized criticality as an absorbing-state phase transition, Physical Review E 57 (1998) 5095–5105. P. Bak, C. Tang and K. Wiesenfeld, Self-organized criticality, Physical Review A 38 (1988) 364–374.
counterexample: The identity fixes the mean of this model only. It does not prove that a natural system with a power law has a sandpile mechanism, and it fixes no exponent. The view of Sornette and his co-authors is an interpretation, not a general theorem. A power law also comes from other mechanisms, such as a mixture of exponential laws or a multiplicative process.
